topic: The Inseparable Duo: The Inverse Relationship Between Derivatives and Integrals
target_audience: High school seniors or first-year university students

sections.title: The Cheetah's Journey: Speed vs. Distance
lecture_lines: Meet our cheetah racing across the savanna.
Speedometer shows its instantaneous speed, the derivative.
Odometer tracks total distance covered, the integral.
animations: Fade in Cheetah [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/cheetah.svg] silhouette (#D4AF37) moving from left to right.
Display a Speedometer (#FFFFFF) in top left; needle fluctuates, label it "Speed (Derivative)" (#00FFFF).
Display an Odometer (#FFFFFF) in top right; digits increase, label it "Distance (Integral)" (#FFD700).

sections.title: Prerequisite Recap: Slope and Area
lecture_lines: Recall that derivatives represent the slope of curves.
In contrast, integrals represent the area under curves.
We will now link these two fundamental concepts.
animations: Draw a green curve (#00FF00); show a magenta tangent line (#FF00FF) sliding along it.
Shade the area under a segment of the green curve (#00FF00) in light green.
Display labels "Slope (Derivative)" and "Area (Integral)" in white (#FFFFFF) with arrows pointing to the visuals.

sections.title: The Accumulation Function
lecture_lines: Imagine a moving curtain sweeping across a graph.
Shaded area grows as the curtain moves right.
This growing area defines the accumulation function.
As input x increases, the total area accumulates.
This function maps points to their total area.
animations: Draw a green curve f(t) (#00FF00) and a vertical white curtain line (#FFFFFF) at t=0.
Move the curtain to the right; fill the area behind it with light green.
Label the shaded region "A(x)" (#00FF00) and show it as a function of the curtain's position.
Start plotting an orange curve A(x) (#FF8C00) in a separate area, tracking the total shaded area.
Highlight the final orange curve A(x) (#FF8C00) as the representation of total accumulation.

sections.title: The Core Insight: How Fast Does Area Grow?
lecture_lines: How fast does this accumulated area actually grow?
Consider a tiny sliver added at position x.
The sliver height is exactly the function's height.
Area added equals height times the tiny width.
The growth rate is the original function's height.
animations: Zoom into the right edge of the shaded area under f(x) (#00FF00).
Introduce a thin yellow rectangle (#FFFF00) of width "dx" at the boundary.
Label the height of the rectangle f(x) (#00FF00) and the width dx (#FFFFFF).
Show the formula "dA = f(x) * dx" in yellow (#FFFF00) next to the sliver.
Transform the formula to "dA/dx = f(x)" and highlight f(x) (#00FF00).

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem: Two Sides of a Coin
lecture_lines: The area's derivative is the original function's height.
Differentiation and integration are inverse operations.
Integrating a rate gives you the total accumulation.
Differentiating accumulation returns the original rate.
They are two sides of the same coin.
animations: Display f(x) (#00FF00) and its accumulation A(x) (#FF8C00) side-by-side.
Draw a cyan arrow labeled "Integrate" (#00FFFF) from f(x) to A(x).
Pulse the A(x) label (#FF8C00) while the "Integrate" arrow is active.
Draw a magenta arrow labeled "Differentiate" (#FF00FF) from A(x) back to f(x).
Show the text "Fundamental Theorem of Calculus" (#FFFFFF) centered between the functions.

sections.title: Application: The Power of the Relationship
lecture_lines: This relationship lets us calculate areas with ease.
Find the anti-derivative to solve complex integrals.
Total distance is simply the anti-derivative of speed.
animations: Plot the curve y=x^2 (#00FF00) and shade the area from 0 to 2.
Display the anti-derivative F(x) = x^3/3 (#FFFFFF) and the evaluation F(2) - F(0).
Replace the area label with the result "8/3" (#FFFF00) and flash it.
